title: Difference of Two Squares
student_objective: I can recognize a difference of two squares, factor it completely, and explain why the conjugate factors work.
teacher_objective: Diagnose pattern-recognition, perfect-square, sign, GCF-first, repeated-factorization, sum-of-squares, verification, and contextual-model errors.

lesson_flow.label: Watch Tolux factor differences of squares

concept_cards.title: Know the pattern
concept_cards.content: A difference of two squares has the form p²-q² and factors as (p-q)(p+q). The two factors are conjugates: same terms, opposite signs.

concept_cards.title: Check all three conditions
concept_cards.content: There must be exactly two terms, subtraction between them, and both terms must be perfect squares. If any condition fails, do not use the difference-of-squares pattern.

concept_cards.title: Factor out a GCF first
concept_cards.content: If the terms share a greatest common factor, remove it before checking the remaining binomial for difference-of-squares structure.

concept_cards.title: Factor completely
concept_cards.content: After using p²-q²=(p-q)(p+q), inspect every factor again. A new factor may itself be another difference of squares.

concept_cards.title: Do not confuse a sum with a difference
concept_cards.content: Over the real numbers, p²+q² is not a difference of squares. Verify a factorization by multiplying the conjugates: the middle terms cancel and p²-q² remains.

items.tutor_behavior: Recognize x²-5², then use (p-q)(p+q).

items.prompt: Is x²+25 a difference of two squares that factors into real linear factors? Answer yes or no.
accepted_answers: no, it is a sum of squares
items.tutor_behavior: The terms are squares, but the operation is addition, not subtraction.
Factor out 3 first, then factor x²-25 as a difference of squares.

solution_steps.explanation: Both terms are perfect squares and they are being subtracted.
Identify the square roots of the two terms.
Multiply to verify that the middle terms cancel.

items.tutor_behavior: Check square roots first, then write conjugate factors with opposite signs.

solution_steps.explanation: The first term is a perfect square.
The second term is also a perfect square.
Use one minus factor and one plus factor.

items.tutor_behavior: Take the square root of each term and use conjugate binomials.

items.prompt: Factor completely over the real numbers: x⁴-81.

solution_steps.explanation: Treat x² as the first square root and 9 as the second.
The first factor is itself another difference of squares.
Over the real numbers, x²+9 is a sum of squares and does not factor further.

items.tutor_behavior: After the first factorization, inspect every factor again before stopping.

hint_steps: Ask: are both terms perfect squares with subtraction between them?

alternate_solution_steps.explanation: Rewrite each term as a square.
The conjugate factors differ only in the sign between the terms.
Multiplication verifies that the middle terms cancel.

items.tutor_behavior: Rewrite 64 as 8², then use the conjugate pattern.

hint_steps: Find the square root of each term before writing any factors.
Use one factor with subtraction and one with addition.

alternate_solution_steps.explanation: The square roots become the two terms in each factor.
Use conjugates so the middle products cancel.

items.tutor_behavior: Do not use 36 and 121 inside the factors; use their square roots 6x and 11.

hint_steps: Before using the square pattern, check for a greatest common factor.

alternate_solution_steps.explanation: The remaining binomial is a difference of squares.
Keep the GCF outside and factor the binomial completely.

items.tutor_behavior: Extract 8 first; then use the difference-of-squares pattern on x²-9.
Use square roots 2x and 5, not coefficients 4 and 25.
Take square roots before forming factors.

hint_steps: Find the GCF before using a special product pattern.
items.tutor_behavior: Factor the GCF first; otherwise the final answer is not completely factored.

items.prompt: Factor completely over the real numbers: x⁴-16.
hint_steps: Treat x² as one square root: x⁴=(x²)².
Factor x²-4 again, but stop at x²+4 over the real numbers.
items.tutor_behavior: Keep checking factors after the first step; x²-4 factors again.
Use square roots 9x and 1.
Factor out 2 before using 9x²-25=(3x-5)(3x+5).

items.prompt: Factor completely over the real numbers: 16x⁴-81.
items.tutor_behavior: First factor (4x²)²-9², then factor 4x²-9 again.

items.prompt: A student says x²+49=(x-7)(x+7). Is the student correct? Answer yes or no.
items.explanation_prompt: Explain why the proposed factors do not match x²+49 and state what (x-7)(x+7) actually equals.
items.explanation_guidance: The conjugate product (x-7)(x+7) equals x²-49, not x²+49. The original expression is a sum of squares and does not factor into real linear factors.
items.tutor_behavior: Require the student to distinguish a sum from a difference and verify the conjugate product.

items.prompt: A square design has area x² square units, and a 6-by-6 square is removed. Factor the remaining area x²-36 to show the two conjugate dimensions used in a rearrangement.
items.tutor_behavior: Recognize x²-6² and interpret the conjugate factors as the resulting dimensions.
Rewrite 100 as 10².
Use square roots 8x and 3.
Recognize (5x)²-1².
Extract 2 before factoring x²-25.
Extract 5 before factoring x²-9.

items.prompt: Factor completely over the real numbers: x⁴-625.
items.tutor_behavior: First factor x⁴-625=(x²-25)(x²+25), then factor x²-25 again.

items.prompt: Does 9x²+16 factor by the difference-of-squares pattern over the real numbers? Answer yes or no.
accepted_answers: no, it is a sum of squares
items.tutor_behavior: Both terms are squares, but the operation is addition.

items.prompt: Multiply (5x-2)(5x+2) to verify the difference-of-squares identity.
items.tutor_behavior: The +10x and -10x middle terms cancel.

items.prompt: A large square has side length 2x and a smaller square of side 3 is removed. Factor the remaining area 4x²-9.
items.tutor_behavior: Use (2x)²-3².

items.prompt: Rewrite 49x²-121 explicitly as p²-q² before factoring.
items.tutor_behavior: Take the square root of each term: 7x and 11.
Extract 3 to get 9x²-1, then use difference of squares.

items.prompt: Factor completely over the real numbers: 100x²-225.
items.tutor_behavior: Extract 25, then factor 4x²-9.

sum_vs_difference.teacher_signal: Applies difference-of-squares factoring to a sum of squares

gcf_first.teacher_signal: Skips the greatest common factor or stops before factoring completely

factor_completely.teacher_signal: Stops after the first difference-of-squares factorization when another factor can be reduced

verification.teacher_signal: Cannot verify that conjugate middle terms cancel
